LIABILITY FOR MISLEADING EMPLOYMENT RECOMMENDATIONS (RANDI W. V. MUROC JOINT UNIFIED SCHOOL DIST.; CIV. CODE §§ 47(C), 1709, 1710, 1714) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says about tort liability for an employment recommendation that praises a former employee while withholding what the recommending employer knows. It draws on the California Supreme Court's decision in Randi W. v. Muroc Joint Unified School Dist. (1997) 14 Cal.4th 1066, which held that a writer of a letter of recommendation owes third persons a duty not to misrepresent a former employee's qualifications and character where the misrepresentation presents a substantial, foreseeable risk of physical injury; on the Civil Code provisions the court worked from — section 1714, subdivision (a) (the general duty of ordinary care), sections 1709 and 1710 (deceit), and section 47, subdivision (c) (the qualified privilege for employer reference communications); and on the Court of Appeal's later decision in P.S. v. San Bernardino City Unified School Dist. (2009) 174 Cal.App.4th 953, which held that later amendments to the Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act did not abrogate the part of Randi W. rejecting a negligence per se theory. Where a specific recommending employer and former employee are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any party named, as a general reference. It states what the statutes and the opinions say. It does not evaluate any particular reference, letter, telephone call, or reference policy, and it does not say what any employer or applicant should do.

THE STATUTORY BACKDROP: ORDINARY CARE AND THE DEFINITION OF DECEIT (CIV. CODE §§ 1714, 1709, 1710)
Three Civil Code provisions supply the vocabulary the California Supreme Court used in Randi W. Section 1714, subdivision (a), states the general responsibility of everyone for injury occasioned to another by want of ordinary care or skill in the management of his or her property or person, subject to the injured person's own want of ordinary care. Section 1709 makes one who willfully deceives another, with intent to induce the other to alter his position to his injury or risk, liable for the resulting damage. Section 1710 then defines “a deceit, within the meaning of the last section,” in four numbered ways; two of them matter to recommendation letters. Subdivision 2 covers the assertion, as a fact, of what is not true by one who has no reasonable ground for believing it true — the form of deceit that corresponds to negligent misrepresentation. Subdivision 3 covers suppression of a fact by one bound to disclose it, and also by one who gives information of other facts which are likely to mislead for want of communication of the suppressed fact — the “half-truth” branch. In Randi W. the court noted that it was considering “liability to a third person injured as a result of the alleged fraud, an extension of ordinary tort liability based on fraud,” and cited section 1709 at that point.

THE QUESTION THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT DECIDED IN RANDI W. V. MUROC JOINT UNIFIED SCHOOL DIST.
Randi W. arose on demurrer. Officers of three school districts that had formerly employed a vice principal wrote recommendations to a college placement office, on forms stating that the information would be sent to prospective employers; the complaint alleged that the writers knew of prior charges or complaints of sexual misconduct with students and said nothing about them, that another district hired the vice principal in reliance on the recommendations, and that he then molested a student of the hiring district. The California Supreme Court opened by stating the question as one about the circumstances in which courts may impose tort liability on employers who fail to use reasonable care in recommending former employees without disclosing material information bearing on their fitness. It then stated its conclusion: the letters, containing unreserved and unconditional praise despite the alleged knowledge of complaints or charges, constituted misleading statements that could form the basis for tort liability for fraud or negligent misrepresentation. The court paired that conclusion with the limiting proposition that ordinarily a recommending employer is not accountable to third persons for failing to disclose negative information, and that liability may be imposed only where the recommendation amounts to an affirmative misrepresentation presenting a foreseeable and substantial risk of physical harm to a third person.

THE RESTATEMENT PROVISIONS THE COURT ADOPTED (REST.2D TORTS, §§ 310, 311)
The Court of Appeal in Randi W. had relied principally on sections 310 and 311 of the Restatement Second of Torts, and the California Supreme Court analyzed the case in those terms. Section 310, addressing intentional conduct, subjects an actor who makes a misrepresentation to liability to another for physical harm resulting from an act done by the other or by a third person in reliance on the truth of the representation, where the actor intends or should realize the statement is likely to induce action involving an unreasonable risk of physical harm and knows the statement is false or that he lacks the knowledge he professes. Section 311, addressing negligent conduct, subjects one who negligently gives false information to another to liability for physical harm caused by action taken by the other in reasonable reliance on the information, where the harm results either to that person or to such third persons as the actor should expect to be put in peril by the action taken, and states that the negligence may consist of a failure to exercise reasonable care in ascertaining the accuracy of the information or in the manner in which it is communicated. The court proceeded by asking whether, in deciding to adopt these two provisions in these circumstances, the complaint sufficiently pleaded duty, breach by misrepresentation or false information, and reasonable reliance by the hiring district that proximately caused the plaintiff's injury.

DUTY: AN ISSUE OF FIRST IMPRESSION ANALYZED UNDER THE ROWLAND FACTORS
The defendants in Randi W. argued that, absent a special relationship or a specific and known threat of harm to the plaintiff, they owed her no duty of care and no obligation to disclose anything about the charges against their former employee. The plaintiff did not contend that a special relationship existed. The court recorded the plaintiff's acknowledgment that no California case had yet held that one who intentionally or negligently provides false information to another owes a duty of care to a third person who neither received the information nor stands in a special relationship with the provider, and treated the issue as one of first impression. It then applied the general analytical principles used to determine duty, beginning from the rule that in California all persons have a duty to use ordinary care to prevent others from being injured as a result of their conduct, and working through the considerations catalogued in Rowland v. Christian — foreseeability of harm, certainty of injury, closeness of the connection between conduct and injury, moral blame, the policy of preventing future harm, the burden on the defendant and the consequences to the community of imposing a duty, and the availability, cost and prevalence of insurance.

FORESEEABILITY AND THE CHAIN OF CAUSATION FROM A REFERENCE TO AN ASSAULT
Applying the duty factors, the court in Randi W. first asked whether the plaintiff's injuries were a foreseeable result of the representations about the former employee's qualifications and character coupled with the failure to disclose the charges of sexual misconduct — posing the question as whether the defendants could reasonably have foreseen that the representations and omissions in their reference letters would result in physical injury to someone. It described the chain of causation running from the statements and omissions to the alleged assault as somewhat attenuated, but concluded the assault was reasonably foreseeable, reasoning in three steps on the facts alleged: that the hiring district's officers would read and rely on the letters in deciding to hire; that, had the recommendation not been unqualified, the district would not have hired him; and that once hired he might injure a student of that district. On moral blame the court said only that the question would depend on the proof at trial, while observing that unreserved recommendations coupled with a failure to disclose facts reasonably necessary to avoid or minimize the risk of further child molestation or abuse could arguably be characterized as morally blameworthy. On insurance it assumed standard business liability coverage would be available for negligent misrepresentation or nondisclosure but not for the fraud or intentional misconduct alleged.

THE ALTERNATIVES THE COURT IDENTIFIED: FULL DISCLOSURE, OR A “NO COMMENT” LETTER
In weighing the burden of imposing a duty, the court in Randi W. identified two courses of conduct it said were available to a recommending employer to avoid tort liability: writing a full disclosure letter revealing all relevant facts about the former employee's background, or writing a no comment letter that omits any affirmative representations about qualifications and merely verifies basic employment dates and details. The court stated that the parties had cited no case or Restatement provision suggesting that a former employer has an affirmative duty of disclosure that would preclude a no comment letter, and restated the background rule that liability may not be imposed for mere nondisclosure or other failure to act, at least absent some special relationship. The court also recorded, without resolving, the competing empirical claim pressed by the defendants and by commentators: that a rule of liability would inhibit the preparation and distribution of reference letters, that many employers had already adopted no comment policies, and that such policies work to the detriment of prospective employers and prospective employees alike.

THE HOLDING AND ITS EXPRESS LIMIT TO RISKS OF PHYSICAL INJURY
The court stated its holding in a single sentence: consistent with sections 310 and 311 of the Restatement Second of Torts, the writer of a letter of recommendation owes to third persons a duty not to misrepresent the facts in describing the qualifications and character of a former employee, if making those misrepresentations would present a substantial, foreseeable risk of physical injury to the third persons. The same paragraph states the converse: absent resulting physical injury, or some special relationship between the parties, the writer of a letter of recommendation should have no duty of care extending to third persons for misrepresentations concerning former employees, and in those cases the policy favoring free and open communication with prospective employers should prevail. The duty the court recognized therefore runs to third persons, not to the recommending employer's former employee and not to the prospective employer as such, and it is defined by the character of the risk the misrepresentation creates rather than by the relationship between the writer and the person injured.

MISLEADING HALF-TRUTHS DISTINGUISHED FROM MERE NONDISCLOSURE
Having found a duty, the court asked whether the letters contained misrepresentations at all, since a writer who says nothing false makes no misrepresentation within sections 310 and 311. The defendants argued that their letters neither discussed nor denied the prior complaints, that a letter noting only favorable qualities cannot reasonably be deemed misleading as to unfavorable ones, and that no reasonable person assumes a recommendation states the whole truth. The court instead treated the case as a misleading half-truths situation: having undertaken to provide some information about the former employee's credentials and character, the writers were obliged to disclose all other facts which materially qualify the limited facts disclosed. Applying that principle, the court concluded that letters essentially recommending the former employee for any position without reservation or qualification constituted affirmative representations that strongly implied he was fit to interact appropriately and safely with female students, and that those representations were false and misleading in light of the alleged knowledge of repeated sexual improprieties. The court supported the half-truth principle with a string of authorities that includes a parenthetical description of Civil Code section 1710, subdivision 3.

WHOSE RELIANCE COUNTS: THE HIRING EMPLOYER'S, NOT THE INJURED PERSON'S
The complaint in Randi W. alleged that the hiring district relied on the letters but said nothing about the plaintiff's own reliance, and the defendants argued that a deceit plaintiff must plead actual reliance on the misrepresentation. The court agreed with the Court of Appeal that the ordinary actual-reliance requirement did not control, holding that under the Restatement provisions the plaintiff need only allege that her injury resulted from action that the recipient of the misrepresentations took in reliance on them. It added the practical observation that in a case involving false or fraudulent letters of recommendation sent to prospective employers about a potentially dangerous employee, it would be unusual for the person ultimately injured to rely on such letters or even to be aware of them. The court also noted that questions about the reasonableness of the hiring district's reliance — including the effect of information the hiring district itself later received — were not before it on demurrer, and that in any event a failure to plead reliance would not support sustaining a demurrer without leave to amend.

THE EMPLOYER REFERENCE PRIVILEGE (CIV. CODE § 47, SUBD. (C)) AND HOW RANDI W. TREATED IT
Civil Code section 47, subdivision (c) makes privileged a communication, without malice, to an interested person by one who is also interested, by one whose relation to the interested person affords reasonable ground for supposing the motive innocent, or by one requested by the interested person to give the information. The subdivision expressly applies to and includes a communication concerning the job performance or qualifications of an applicant for employment, based upon credible evidence, made without malice, by a current or former employer to, and upon request of, one whom the employer reasonably believes is a prospective employer of the applicant. In Randi W. the plaintiff invoked this provision to answer the argument that tort liability would chill references, and an amicus curiae argued that the privilege reached beyond defamation actions and would defeat the misrepresentation claim. The court did not decide that question. San Bernardino City Unified School Dist. (2009) 174 Cal.App.4th 953, which held that later amendments to the Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act did not abrogate the part of Randi W. rejecting a negligence per se theory. Where a specific recommending employer and former employee are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any party named, as a general reference. Three Civil Code provisions supply the vocabulary the California Supreme Court used in Randi W. Section 1714, subdivision (a), states the general responsibility of everyone for injury occasioned to another by want of ordinary care or skill in the management of his or her property or person, subject to the injured person's own want of ordinary care. Section 1709 makes one who willfully deceives another, with intent to induce the other to alter his position to his injury or risk, liable for the resulting damage. Subdivision 2 covers the assertion, as a fact, of what is not true by one who has no reasonable ground for believing it true — the form of deceit that corresponds to negligent misrepresentation. Subdivision 3 covers suppression of a fact by one bound to disclose it, and also by one who gives information of other facts which are likely to mislead for want of communication of the suppressed fact — the “half-truth” branch. In Randi W. the court noted that it was considering “liability to a third person injured as a result of the alleged fraud, an extension of ordinary tort liability based on fraud,” and cited section 1709 at that point.

expectedJSON.body: The court stated its holding in a single sentence: consistent with sections 310 and 311 of the Restatement Second of Torts, the writer of a letter of recommendation owes to third persons a duty not to misrepresent the facts in describing the qualifications and character of a former employee, if making those misrepresentations would present a substantial, foreseeable risk of physical injury to the third persons. The same paragraph states the converse: absent resulting physical injury, or some special relationship between the parties, the writer of a letter of recommendation should have no duty of care extending to third persons for misrepresentations concerning former employees, and in those cases the policy favoring free and open communication with prospective employers should prevail. The duty the court recognized therefore runs to third persons, not to the recommending employer's former employee and not to the prospective employer as such, and it is defined by the character of the risk the misrepresentation creates rather than by the relationship between the writer and the person injured.

expectedJSON.body: Having found a duty, the court asked whether the letters contained misrepresentations at all, since a writer who says nothing false makes no misrepresentation within sections 310 and 311. The defendants argued that their letters neither discussed nor denied the prior complaints, that a letter noting only favorable qualities cannot reasonably be deemed misleading as to unfavorable ones, and that no reasonable person assumes a recommendation states the whole truth. The court instead treated the case as a misleading half-truths situation: having undertaken to provide some information about the former employee's credentials and character, the writers were obliged to disclose all other facts which materially qualify the limited facts disclosed. Applying that principle, the court concluded that letters essentially recommending the former employee for any position without reservation or qualification constituted affirmative representations that strongly implied he was fit to interact appropriately and safely with female students, and that those representations were false and misleading in light of the alleged knowledge of repeated sexual improprieties. The court supported the half-truth principle with a string of authorities that includes a parenthetical description of Civil Code section 1710, subdivision 3.

The court agreed with the Court of Appeal that the ordinary actual-reliance requirement did not control, holding that under the Restatement provisions the plaintiff need only allege that her injury resulted from action that the recipient of the misrepresentations took in reliance on them. It added the practical observation that in a case involving false or fraudulent letters of recommendation sent to prospective employers about a potentially dangerous employee, it would be unusual for the person ultimately injured to rely on such letters or even to be aware of them. The court also noted that questions about the reasonableness of the hiring district's reliance — including the effect of information the hiring district itself later received — were not before it on demurrer, and that in any event a failure to plead reliance would not support sustaining a demurrer without leave to amend.

The subdivision expressly applies to and includes a communication concerning the job performance or qualifications of an applicant for employment, based upon credible evidence, made without malice, by a current or former employer to, and upon request of, one whom the employer reasonably believes is a prospective employer of the applicant. expectedJSON.body: Randi W. was not a complete victory for the plaintiff. She had also pleaded negligence per se, alleging that the school districts breached a mandatory duty under the Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act to report the earlier incidents, and the Court of Appeal had allowed that count. The Supreme Court reversed on that count. It said it need not decide whether the allegations sufficed to show the defendants knew or suspected reportable child abuse, because the plaintiff was not a member of the class for whose protection the Reporting Act was enacted: the defendant districts were never her custodians, and so owed her no obligations under the act. Reading the act to reach her would, the court said, impose a broader reporting obligation than the Legislature intended, because a custodian that failed to report abuse of one child in its care could be held liable years later to any other children abused by the same person. The disposition accordingly affirmed the Court of Appeal as to the negligent misrepresentation and fraud counts and reversed as to the negligence per se count. Justice Kennard, joined by Justices Baxter and Werdegar, concurred in the rest of the opinion but dissented from that part, concluding that the plaintiff had adequately pleaded negligence per se and that the act's stated purpose of protecting children from abuse carries no qualification limiting it to children in the reporting party's care.
